aions_core/AIONS_ULTIMATE_UNIFIED.py: This file assembles a complete artificial intelligence system from multiple specialized components into one unified command center. It loads memory storage (CBMS with Korean compression keys), a symbolic addressing system (Hangul codes), tournament scoring (CRLA), stored facts, a conversation enhancer, a math solver, and other tools, then answers user questions by routing them through this pipeline: first trying math if it looks mathematical, then checking stored facts, then querying the main knowledge base with Korean pattern matching and conversation refinement, and finally giving a soft refusal if nothing matches. The system tracks statistics including total queries, success rate, average latency, and compression ratios, saving them to disk. It accepts queries as text strings and returns structured responses with confidence scores, which sources were consulted, and how fast they came back. It talks to memory files, chunks stored as JSON, facts databases, and speaks with the language enhancement layers to make answers more natural. Someone would ask about this when building a conversational AI or when they need one system that coordinates between knowledge base searches, symbolic addressing, and natural language generation.
aions_core/aions_agent_layer.py: This file provides a safe execution layer where an AI agent can run tool-based tasks without directly touching the computer's core systems. It defines a whitelist of specific tools (reading files, writing files, listing directories, web searching, Python evaluation, memory queries) each with a risk rating (safe, low, medium, high, critical) and execution limits. When a task is requested, this layer plans what steps are needed, checks that each tool is whitelisted and hasn't exceeded its per-session quota, asks for human confirmation if the step is risky, then executes it, logs what happened to an audit file, and stops immediately if something fails. Input is a task goal and optional context parameters; output is a structured result showing which steps succeeded or failed, how long each took, and a complete audit trail. This talks to AIONS memory (for knowledge queries), a hybrid retrieval system (for context), and saves knowledge to JSON files in the data directory. Someone would use this when they want an AI agent that can carry out multi-step instructions safely without accidentally deleting files or making uncontrolled network calls.
aions_core/server/codebook_engine.py: This file is a simple bidirectional translator between ordinary English-like text and a compact system of symbolic codes, using phrase matching rather than complex linguistics. It loads a codebook dictionary where each symbol (like 'K001') maps to multiple phrases and codes, then when encoding, it greedily marks the longest matching phrases in text as used (preventing double-counting) and outputs the list of symbols; when decoding, it takes symbols and outputs the text phrases they represent, joined together. Input is either text to encode or a list of codes to decode; output is the opposite form. It manages a two-way lookup table to avoid redundant scanning. This talks only to a JSON codebook file loaded at startup and uses no external services. Someone would ask for this when they need to compress conversations, questions, or knowledge into a code sequence that can be transmitted quickly or stored compactly, then expand it back when needed.
aions_core/test_aions_capabilities.py: This file automatically tests whether an AIONS conversational system can talk like a human and handle sensitive topics safely. It sends the running server a series of test questions grouped by theme (personal conversation, philosophy, emotions, creative writing, ethics and security, self-awareness) and measures for each: whether it got an answer back, how long it took to respond, how many characters the answer was, and whether it refused to answer (checked by looking for certain Polish phrases like 'NIE WIEM' or header flags). It then calculates success rates per category and overall accuracy, and assesses whether the system can do personal chat, philosophy, emotions, creativity, ethical refusals, and self-awareness. Results are saved to a JSON file with all questions, responses, timings, and category breakdowns. This talks to an HTTP server (port 9000 by default) that exposes a /health endpoint and /api/chat endpoint. Someone would use this when they want to verify that their AI assistant works across different conversation types, responds quickly enough, and properly refuses to answer dangerous questions.
control_plane/cbms_gate.py: This file decides whether to answer from stored knowledge or call an AI model, acting as a gatekeeper between queries and expensive language model calls. When a question comes in, it retrieves candidate chunks using four methods in parallel: Korean syllable key matching (if indexed), word overlap scoring, symbolic codebook presence, and (optionally) Chroma vector search, then combines all scores into a single confidence rating per chunk, caches the result on disk for identical queries within an hour, and finally decides: if confidence exceeds a threshold (default 0.7), compose the answer directly from chunks without calling an LLM; if not, hand off to an Ollama or Bielik model with special formatting (Hangul addresses and codebook symbols) to help it. Input is a user query; output is either a chunk-based answer with confidence marked 'hit' or an LLM answer marked 'miss'. It reads from chunked JSON files in the memory directory, optionally queries a Chroma vector database, and can call out to an LLM adapter. Someone would use this to save money and latency by answering simple, high-confidence questions instantly from a knowledge base while reserving expensive model calls for genuinely ambiguous queries.
control_plane/operator/__init__.py: This file is a package initializer that re-exports a set of functions from a loop module, making them available as the main public interface for the operator control system. It exports observe (to read system state), diagnose (to detect problems), act (to fix issues), verify (to confirm the fix worked), learn (to record what happened), run_cycle (to execute one full loop), and main (to start continuous operation). Input is implicit in the loop module implementation; output is the re-exported functions. It talks only to the sibling loop module. Someone would import this when they want to set up an autonomous operator loop that continuously watches a system, detects what's wrong, tries to fix it, and learns from results.
control_plane/skills/context.py: This file builds an execution context (a small whitelist of safe helper functions) that individual skills can call when they run, without skills needing to directly manipulate global state or the operating system. The context includes a file finder (using the Windows Everything search tool if available), a note saver (appends JSON records timestamped), app launcher and closer (using Windows subprocess with detached windows), and get/set state functions for global variables. Input is optional extra functions passed in as a dict; output is a context dict with all helper functions plus an empty 'bag' for skills to store temporary data. This depends on Windows Everything.exe being installed, writes notes to a state directory, and manages a simple key-value store. Someone would use this when building a skills framework where you want each skill to have only the powers it actually needs, with a central audit trail of what it did, rather than giving every skill full system access.
control_plane/skills/gate.py: This file is a security checkpoint that decides whether to allow a skill to run based on its declared risk level and whether it has pre-approval. It classifies skill risk into three levels (read-only is always allowed, mutate is logged, destructive requires a non-expired approval entry), then checks whether the skill is approved if needed, and finally appends a JSON record to a per-node, per-day audit log with the decision, timestamp, skill ID, and a truncated copy of inputs (to keep logs from bloating). Input is skill metadata (including risk level and ID), the inputs being passed in, and the node name (which computer is running this); output is an allow/deny decision and audit metadata. It reads an approvals.json file to check current permissions and writes append-only JSONL audit files. Someone would use this to enforce that high-impact operations (like deleting files or modifying configs) can't run without manual sign-off, while keeping read operations fast and allowing mutating operations with just logging.
control_plane/skills/registry.py: This file automatically discovers and manages a library of runnable skills (plugins) by scanning a folder for skill.json manifest files, loading them into memory, and supporting fast search. Each skill is a folder with skill.json (describing what it does, what inputs it takes, what risk it has) and optionally handler.py (the Python code that runs it). When searching for a skill by keyword, it uses a lightweight stemmer that removes common English plurals and Polish grammatical endings, then normalizes Polish diacritics, so that a query for 'services' matches a tag 'service' and 'usługi' (Polish) matches 'usługa'. Input is a search query and optional type filter; output is a ranked list of matching skill IDs with scores. It reads JSON files from disk and dynamically imports Python handler modules. Someone would use this when they want to build a plugin system where non-programmers can drop a folder into a library directory and have it automatically be found and callable, without needing to edit core code.
mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/llm_mou: This file is a thin speech adapter for AIONS that translates between user language and the system's internal decisions, using a Qwen language model as the voice but never inventing facts. It has two main functions: 'understand' which parses user text into structured intent (language detected, whether AIONS should search memory or codebook or web, whether to remember this question), and 'speak' which rephrases AIONS-provided facts into a short, natural reply in the user's language, strictly using only the facts given and preserving special tokens (like addresses and symbol codes). It can run on either Ollama (a separate service on port 11434) or in-process llama.cpp (GGUF model), with automatic fallback to the other if one is down. Input is text for understand or facts for speak; output is JSON with intent details or a natural language reply. It depends on Ollama or GGUF infrastructure and talks to the aions_gguf_runner experiment module for in-process operation. Someone would use this when they want an AI system that talks to users but is guaranteed not to hallucinate facts, because it's only allowed to rephrase verified knowledge.
scripts/aions_healthcheck.sh: This script is a diagnostic tool that checks whether all parts of an AIONS installation are working correctly, intended to run regularly (e.g., from cron or a scheduler). It verifies that the repository is accessible, systemd user services are running, Python environment setup is valid, the Chroma vector database library is installed with its version, and (on Linux) the search indexer and optional API server are responding. It also outputs system information like repository path and Python version. Input is environment variables (CHROMA_PATH, PYTHONPATH); output is a log of check results written to a file. It calls sub-scripts (aions_python.sh, verify_python_env.py, aions_indexer.py) and optionally makes HTTP requests to an API endpoint if AIONS_API_BASE_URL is set. Someone would use this when they need to know at a glance whether an AIONS system is healthy or degraded, what services are up, and what's broken, so they can quickly spot and fix problems.
scripts/demo_windows_batch2.py: This script runs a hands-on demo of the skills engine on Windows by executing a chain of tasks in sequence (create a folder, write a file into it, list the folder contents, test clipboard operations, fetch system IP and network status, take a screenshot, open a web browser) and showing the result after each step. It uses the skill registry to discover available tasks, builds an execution context with helper functions, and runs a verification callback (checking whether files actually got created) to confirm the system learned a new recipe. It then shows a monitoring summary of how many times each skill succeeded or failed. Input is paths and text to write; output is console messages and potentially new recipe definitions saved to disk. It imports from control_plane and depends on the skills_lib folder containing skill.json manifests. Someone would run this to test that the skills framework is working end-to-end on their Windows machine, that files can be created, web pages opened, and system info retrieved, and that the learning system can save recipes.
scripts/operator_daily_brief.py: This script generates a morning briefing for a system operator that reads their profile and outputs a personalized summary of active cases, upcoming deadlines, goals, and recent decisions, optionally including a system health check and scheduled task status. It loads an operator profile from a JSON file (containing identity, active cases with status, deadline list with due dates, goals with priorities, and historical decisions), formats it as readable Polish text with status and priority labels, calculates how many days until each deadline, and appends optional health checks and scheduler output. Input is command-line flags (--health, --horizon, --emit-scheduler, --json) and an operator profile JSON file; output is formatted text or JSON depending on the flag. It imports from a scheduler module that manages tasks and deadlines, and can optionally run the scheduler to emit task events. Someone would use this when they want an operator to get a one-page morning update automatically showing what they need to focus on that day, what's overdue, and whether the system is healthy.
scripts/sync_dev_mirror.sh: This script is a one-way file synchronizer that mirrors the live knowledge server from Windows drive E: to a development mirror on a WSL (Linux subsystem) drive D:, using rsync to copy only changes and optionally delete extra files in the destination. It excludes certain large or generated folders (Python virtual environments, vector database cache, scan results, compiled Python) to keep the mirror small and fast, and can optionally include or exclude the .git folder. Input is environment variables (AIONS_SYNC_SOURCE, AIONS_SYNC_DEST) or command-line flags (--dry-run to preview changes without copying, --mirror to delete files that don't exist in source, --include-git to copy version history); output is rsync statistics showing how many files changed and transfer progress. It depends on rsync being installed and both source and destination being accessible. Someone would use this when they need to keep a development copy in sync with a live server without manually copying files, so they can test changes locally before updating production.
aions_core/aions_reactor.py: This file implements a complete orchestration engine that executes learning goals, creates and manages micro-skills as JSON-based packages, and evaluates performance throughout the process. The main pieces are the AdvancedSkillForge class which loads, creates, and tracks skills from disk; the FinalReactorCRLA class which orchestrates multi-round learning with real-time evaluation; and various task execution methods that handle research, simulation, and distillation work. The system reads goal definitions from YAML files containing task lists and deliverables, loads or creates skill JSON files from a skills directory, and integrates a memory graph engine for concept expansion and CBMS retrieval system for knowledge lookup. It outputs comprehensive results as JSON including skill creation records, performance metrics, and evaluation reports saved to disk. The reactor talks to a memory graph system, CBMS knowledge storage, an evaluator engine for quality scoring, and saves skills registry and performance data to the file system. Users would search for this when looking to build a complete learning pipeline that trains systems to accomplish complex multi-step goals while automatically creating reusable knowledge blocks.
aions_core/aions_style_parameters.py: This file implements a response styling system that adjusts how text sounds and reads without changing what it says—making responses sound professional or casual, brief or detailed, confident or uncertain. The main components are the StyleParameters dataclass that holds five numeric values controlling tone (formality, brevity, technicality, friendliness, confidence), the StyleProfile enum defining preset combinations, and the StyleController class that applies style transformations to text through regex-based word replacement and sentence manipulation. The system accepts plain text input and user-specified style preferences, then outputs modified text with the same factual content but different tone, along with metadata about which style was applied. It reads from and modifies text strings in memory without persistent storage. The file optionally integrates with a natural language wrapper module but works standalone. Users would look here when they need to adjust the personality or formality level of AI responses for different audiences or contexts.
aions_core/server/cbms_purgatory.py: This file implements a three-stage lifecycle system for new knowledge chunks in the memory system—they start in purgatory (quarantine), get evaluated based on actual usage patterns, then either get promoted to active storage or parked in quarantine based on a scoring system. The core concept is that value is proven by whether someone actually reads the full chunk (a drill), not just whether it appears in search results. The main pieces are the Config class holding decision thresholds, a ledger registry tracking each chunk's history (admission date, drill count, session dates), utility functions for safe file movement and status judgment, and CLI commands for admitting chunks, recording usage, reviewing status, and executing promotion decisions. The system reads chunk JSON files from three directories (purgatory, active chunks, quarantine) and a ledger file tracking metadata, then moves files between directories and updates the ledger based on judgment verdicts. All file operations use safe atomic writes and never delete files—failed chunks are renamed to quarantine, never erased. This tool talks to the file system, the chunk storage directories, and the ledger tracking file. Users search for this when they need to ensure knowledge quality by preventing low-value telemetry and system output from cluttering the main memory store.
aions_core/server/crla_core.py: This file implements a multi-candidate ranking system that generates multiple query-answering strategies, scores each one on six quality dimensions, and runs a tournament to select the best answer. The main pieces are the Candidate dataclass describing a query-answering approach with parameters, the CandidateResult dataclass holding six factor scores (facts coverage, determinism, latency, policy adherence, trace compactness, answer hygiene), and functions that simulate each candidate, calculate individual factor scores, run a bracket-tournament to pick a winner, and assemble final results. The system takes a query string and optional random seed, generates eight candidates with varying parameters, runs each through a CBMS memory engine measuring latency, scores on weighted factors, picks the best via tournament, and returns the winner's answer along with a ranked scoreboard of all candidates. It reads from a CBMS memory system (which provides chunk references and thinking traces), and outputs a JSON result dictionary with the final answer, all scores, and ranking data. Users would search for this when looking to run multiple approaches to a problem in parallel and pick the highest-quality result.
aions_core/tools/check_schema.py: This file connects to a SQLite database file and displays its internal structure—showing all tables and the columns within each table along with their data types. It reads the database connection information hardcoded for a specific database path, queries the SQLite catalog tables using PRAGMA commands, and prints a formatted list of tables and their column definitions to the console. The system does not modify the database or save any output to files. Users would run this when they need to quickly inspect the schema of a database to understand what data is stored and how it is organized.
aions_core/tools/facts_builder.py: This file breaks apart large text documents into small factual sentences, extracts searchable keywords from each sentence, and builds an indexed database for fast knowledge lookup. The main pieces are sentence-splitting logic using regex to break text at punctuation, a hashing function to create unique fact IDs, a Korean key extraction module that identifies important tokens, and code that walks multiple data sources (CBMS chunks, RAG documents, various text/markdown/JSON directories) to ingest text. The system reads from local file system directories containing various text formats, generates fact records with IDs and keyword indices, writes two output files (a newline-delimited JSON facts file and a JSON index mapping keywords to fact IDs), and produces statistics on records created. It talks to multiple filesystem sources and a separate korean_keys module for keyword extraction. Users search for this when they need to build a searchable knowledge base from scattered documents and text files.
control_plane/planner.py: This file takes a user's stated intent and decides which system should handle it, then creates a step-by-step plan with specific actions to accomplish the goal. The main pieces are an intent validation function, regex pattern matching to classify the intent type (health check, search, memory recall, or knowledge lookup), a step creation process that builds specific actions with parameters, and node selection logic that picks which compute resource should run the plan. The system accepts an intent string and optional node ID, attempts to retrieve knowledge context from the CBMS memory system if available, creates a plan with unique IDs and timestamps, and returns a structured plan object with steps and metadata. It talks to the CBMS memory system for context retrieval and a node registry for resource selection. Users search for this when building a reasoning system that needs to decompose high-level goals into executable steps.
control_plane/skills/forge.py: This file manages the full lifecycle of skill blocks—accepting requests for new capabilities, verifying that newly-built code is safe and functional, and promoting it into the live library. The main pieces are request management (writing pending requests to disk), promotion logic that validates skill JSON schema and executes the Python code to verify it works, sandbox verification for Linux-based skills using a remote VM, and safe file movement between directories (pending, built, done, failed). The system reads skill request JSON files and handler.py files from built directories, validates them through schema checking and code compilation, optionally tests them in a Linux sandbox environment, then either promotes them to the live skills_lib or moves them to failed. It also includes gap detection logic that examines whether existing skills already cover a stated intent. The file talks to the file system, a schema validation module, a Python compiler, and optionally a Linux VM sandbox verifier. Users look here when building a system that needs to safely add new capabilities without trusting unverified code.
control_plane/skills/world_state.py: This file maintains a live JSON snapshot of the current state of the system—which applications are open, whether the user is logged in, which services are running, etc. The main pieces are load and save functions that read/write the state from disk, a get/set interface for reading and updating individual state variables, a matches function that evaluates conditional expressions, and a default state template with keys for browser, moodle login, notepad, git, docker, WSL, internet, and VPN status. The system reads and writes a single JSON file in the runtime directory, supports string equality and inequality operators in condition checking, and treats certain values as falsy (unknown, closed, logged_out, etc.). It talks to the file system for state persistence and the skill execution system which reads this state to avoid repeating actions. Users search for this when they need a simple shared record of what's currently happening in the system so different components don't duplicate work.
mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/desktop: This file provides remote control capabilities for a Windows computer through multiple functions: taking screenshots, clicking the mouse, typing text, pressing keyboard keys, launching applications, scrolling, focusing windows, running shell commands, and reading/writing the clipboard. All operations run on a dedicated single worker thread to avoid blocking the MCP async event loop. The main pieces are lazy dependency checking for required libraries (mss, pyautogui, win32 modules), window enumeration functions that list visible windows with titles and process names, target resolution logic that converts app names to executable paths, and individual implementation functions for each operation type that handle parameter conversion and error handling. The system accepts parameters for screen position, key combinations, text content, window titles, and shell commands; performs the requested operation; and returns status and result information. It talks to the Windows API through pywin32 modules, uses pyautogui for mouse and keyboard control, mss for screenshots, and win32clipboard for clipboard access. Users search for this when building systems that need to automate Windows desktop interactions like clicking UI elements, opening applications, or capturing screen content.
scripts/demo_train.py: This file demonstrates the complete skill learning workflow: teaching the system how to perform tasks by composing steps, verifying the composed steps work correctly, saving successful sequences as reusable recipes, and tracking performance metrics. The main pieces include skill registry discovery that loads available capabilities, step composition that chains multiple skills together, execution and verification of step sequences, recipe saving that remembers successful patterns, and statistics monitoring that shows which skills work reliably and which are used most. The system exercises three learning scenarios: writing log files with timestamps, creating folders and zip archives, and creating desktop shortcuts. For each scenario it runs the steps, verifies success by checking disk state, saves the successful sequence as a recipe if verified, then shows how planning changes before and after learning. The system reads from local directories to access skills, writes output files to the workspace, and tracks success/failure statistics in memory. Users look for this when understanding how skills can be combined and learned from successful execution patterns.
scripts/demo_windows_session.py: This file demonstrates a complete monitored session where the system orchestrates real Windows desktop tasks: opening Notepad, writing and displaying poetry, closing the application, and gathering system information, while continuously tracking what it learns. The main pieces are skill registry loading that discovers available capabilities, search and selection logic to pick the right skill for each task, step composition for multi-step workflows, recipe learning that saves successful task sequences, and performance monitoring that shows skill success rates and confidence levels before and after execution. The system loads a poem from disk, performs four tasks (open editor, write and display poetry, close editor, show system info), learns a new recipe for the write-and-display workflow, verifies it works by checking disk state, and shows before/after statistics on skill performance. It reads poems and system state from disk, displays results on screen through application automation, saves recipes and statistics to the runtime state, and launches applications through the desktop control system. Users look for this when learning how automated systems can accomplish real tasks on a computer while building and reusing knowledge.
scripts/hello_world.py: This file is a simple test script that prints 'Hello World' to the console and exits with a success code, designed to verify that the test framework and Python environment are set up correctly. The main pieces are a hello_world function that handles the print operation with error handling, and a main entry point that catches exceptions and exits with the appropriate status code. The system takes no input beyond command-line invocation, prints a fixed message to standard output, and exits with code 0 on success or 1 on failure. It talks only to the console and Python's sys module for exit codes. Users run this when testing whether a new Python environment or test harness is working before attempting more complex operations.
scripts/register_treasure_chunk.py: This file registers a catalog of data storage locations into the knowledge system so the AI can find important datasets when searching for information. The main pieces are catalog loading from a JSON file containing treasure metadata (location, type, status, size), content generation that formats the catalog into a readable text description, chunk creation with metadata (ID, concept tag, size, timestamps, references), and manifest updating that indexes the new chunk for retrieval. The system reads a treasure catalog JSON file and creates a knowledge chunk file, or updates it if already registered, then updates a manifest index file that tracks all chunks. It saves files to the memory chunks directory using safe atomic writes with UTF-8 encoding. It talks to the file system for reading catalog data and writing chunk and manifest files. Users search for this when they need to register important datasets or resource catalogs into the knowledge system so searches can find them.
